precision-buffer-settles-not-bandwidth.note: Re-read sprpeo2 p5, p6, p7, p8, p25, p26 and p27, sboa586a p25 and opa333 p7, re-ran the ppm scan myself and re-did the arithmetic. The ppm defect that refuted this record last pass is gone and the replacement is correct and correctly labelled. THE SCAN REPRODUCES EXACTLY. Case-insensitive search for the string ppm over every page of all four ledger PDFs: sprpeo2 0 hits in 54 pages, sboa586a 0 in 27, sboa418 0 in 14 - 95 pages, zero hits - and opa333 exactly 1 hit, on p24, the line 20-ppm/Degrees C Max, 100-uA, SOT23-3 Series Voltage Reference, REF3130, which is an advertisement for a different part and not a settling claim. The p25 source note states precisely that (The slide states no error in ppm - the string ppm appears nowhere in sprpeo2, sboa418 or sboa586a - so any ppm equivalence in this record is arithmetic on the sourced formula, not a vendor claim), so the record now discloses the provenance instead of implying a vendor number. THE ARITHMETIC IS RIGHT. ln(2^16) = 11.0904; exp(-11.0904) = 1.5259e-5 = 2^-16 = 15.26 ppm, i.e. 11.09 tau leaves exactly one 16-bit LSB, which is what rule.bw_min now says; 1/2 LSB = 2^-17 needs -ln(2^-17) = 11.7835 tau, the record's 11.8 in the rule and 11.78 in the note; and this block's 8 ppm target needs -ln(8e-6) = 11.7361 tau, the note's 11.74. The solve ln(1/err) for any other target instruction generalises it correctly. THE SOURCED FORMULA IS ON THE PAGE. sprpeo2 p25 reads For N-bit accuracy BW approximately ln(2^N)/(2*pi*t_settle), For 16-bit BW approximately 11/(2*pi*t_settle), Driver must settle to 16-bit accuracy to 1/2 LSB, Settling time < acquisition time + margin, For 5 MSPS with 70ns acquisition Required closed-loop BW approximately 25 MHz min, Added margin in consideration for signal BW and input RC filter, and the footnote simulating RC combo still recommended - so closed_form_is a floor is the slide's own hedge. EVERY OTHER CITATION RE-READ. p5 carries the SAR internal model with V_CSH(t) = V_CSH(t0) + [VIN - V_CSH(t0)]*(1 - exp(-t/tau)) and tau = R_SH*C_SH, the curve settling inside 1/2 LSB during t_AQ. p7 is exactly as described and this is the claim that most needed re-checking: the figure is a blue dashed box labelled ADC chip containing ONLY the S/H switch, R_SH, C_SH and a block marked ADC - no amplifier - the trace to its right is labelled C_SH voltage, dips at switch closure, recovers and is annotated settled within 1/2 LSB under a t_acq bracket, and the bullets above give the sample-hold capacitor needs to be settled to 1/2 LSB within the ADC acquisition time and t_acq = 1/f_smpl - t_conv_max. The word slew appears nowhere on that page, so the record's insistence that the recovery is the R_SH*C_SH exponential and not an amplifier moving is the page's own content. p8 reads If CSH is not settled to 1/2 LSB within tacq, the ADC sampled waveform will be distorted and attenuated, over an ADC Input Waveform and ADC Output Waveform pair - the record's gloss as gain and linearity error rather than noise is a fair reading of distorted and attenuated. p26 is the charge-bucket panel (main purpose handle the kickback current when a SAR ADC sampling switch closes, quickly charge, must be optimized for settling time). p27 gives practical t_FLT_settle = t_ACQ = 12*tau_FLT, R_FLT = t_ACQ/(12*C_FLT) and Minimum driver GBW > 4*(1/(2*pi*R_FLT*C_FLT)) word for word, which is rule.also_required. sboa586a p25 step 7 is verbatim and is the seventh and last step, so slew being a standalone screen rather than part of the acquisition waveform is the page's own ordering. opa333 p7 confirms SR 0.16 V/us at G = +1 and GBW 350 kHz at C_L = 100 pF. For a principle-level record with three records generalizing onto it I looked specifically for anything left unsourced in the rule block and found none: every field traces to p5, p7, p25, p26, p27 or sboa586a p25, and the one piece of arithmetic is now flagged as arithmetic. Verified.

precision-buffer-zero-drift-speed-vs-imp.note: Re-read sboa586a p26 and p25 and opa333 p7 and p10, pushing on the edited lead-in, and re-measured fig 14 out of the vector geometry rather than by eye. The edit is true of the page and the rest of the record still stands. TABLE 9-1 RE-TRANSCRIBED IN FULL from p26, all eight rows and seven columns: header A Device, B Offset (uV), C Drift (uV/C), D GBW (MHz), E N (nV/rtHz), F MAX Recommended R_IN and Rf||Rg (kohm), G Noise Optimized Rf||Rg (kohm). OPA189 3 / 0.02 / 14 / 5.2 / 1 / 0.183; OPA388 5 / 0.05 / 10 / 7 / 10 / 0.331; OPA333 10 / 0.05 / 0.35 / 55 / 1000 / 20.4; OPA187 10 / 0.015 / 0.55 / 15 / 500 / 15.2; OPA188 25 / 0.085 / 2 / 8.8 / 10 / 0.523; OPA186 10 / 0.04 / 0.75 / 40 / 500 / 10.8; OPA182 4 / 0.012 / 5 / 5.7 / 10 / 0.219; OPA387 2 / 0.012 / 5.7 / 8.5 / 10 / 0.488. THE EDITED CLAIM CHECKS OUT where the old one did not. Ordering the eight parts by column F gives ceilings 1000, 500, 500, 10, 10, 10, 10, 1 kohm against GBWs 0.35, 0.55, 0.75, 2, 5, 5.7, 10, 14 MHz - monotone in opposite directions with no inversion anywhere, so ranking by source-impedance ceiling really is the reverse of ranking by bandwidth. The old lead-in on offset was not: column B runs 3, 5, 10, 10, 25, 10, 4, 2 and does not anti-correlate with D at all (OPA387 is 2 uV at 5.7 MHz while OPA188 is 25 uV at 2 MHz). Both anchor rows in the prose are exact - OPA333 has the widest ceiling at 1000 kohm together with the lowest GBW in the table at 0.35 MHz and the highest noise in column E at 55 nV/rtHz, and OPA189 at 14 MHz and 5.2 nV/rtHz is capped at 1 kohm - and column F does span three decades, 1 to 1000 kohm. ONE IMPRECISION, flagged and not load-bearing: the printed ROW ORDER is OPA189, OPA388, OPA333, OPA187, OPA188, OPA186, OPA182, OPA387, which is sorted by neither F nor D nor B, so the lead-in's phrase the vendor table that ranks them by source-impedance ceiling has to be read as the table's COLUMNS ranking them, not as the order the rows are printed in. The sentence supports that reading (the same table gives both rankings and they are opposite), rule.trade states it unambiguously, and the substance is exactly what the page shows, so this is a wording note rather than a refutation - and worth not churning further, since the record already moved once on a reader's advisory. THE REST RE-CHECKED. p25 keeps the gates separate as the record says: step 2 screens source impedance against column F, step 3 noise against column G, step 6 chopper noise, and step 7 is the seventh and last - Finally, assuming all other criteria are acceptable, check all other amplifier specifications. For example, is bandwidth, slew rate, and output drive meeting your application specific requirements - so speed being screened last is the page's own ordering. opa333 p7 confirms Gain-bandwidth product CL = 100 pF 350 kHz and Slew rate G = +1 0.16 V/us. Fig 14 on p10 re-measured independently off the two bezier paths against the frame (x 359.04 = gain 1 to 527.49 = gain 100 over two decades, y 569.02 = 0 us to 454.90 = 600 us): the 0.01 percent curve starts at 40.4 us at unity gain and rises to 390.0 us at gain 100, and the 0.001 percent curve starts at 50.5 us and rises to 499.3 us, so the record's about 40 us and 50 us at unity gain and rising steeply with gain are both exact and the 100 us envelope bound is anchored on real numbers. The datasheet mislabels that x axis Gain (dB) while the scale runs 1 to 100 over two decades; calling the left edge unity gain is right either way. The closing arithmetic is consistent - 2.048 V divided by 0.16 V/us is 12.80 us. Verified.

precision-buffer-zero-drift-source-imped.note: Re-read sboa586a p11, p17, p18, p19 and p26 and opa333 p7 and p9 visually, pushing on the sentence that changed. Fig 3-5 on p11 settles it: the body text says the two large transients correspond to transitioning of the calibration circuit input switches and that the period of the calibration cycle for this example is 1.54 us (f_chop = 650 kHz), the figure annotates 770ns as a double-headed arrow between the two large 2 uA spikes, and the clock trace below annotates 1.54us (650kHz) across the full period - so two per 1.54 us calibration cycle and annotated 770 ns apart is now exactly what the page shows, which is what the earlier wording got loose. The rest re-checked from scratch and holds: 2 uA against I_B average 160 pA is 12,500 times the bias current in the pages own words, and the closing sentence is that since these transients are currents the impact can be minimized by reducing source and feedback impedance. p17 fig 5-5 is OPA388 offset vs source resistance, flat near 4 uV out to about 10 kohm under the label Op-amp offset dominates and rising to about 400 uV at 1000 kohm under Ib_transients x Rin dominate; table 5-1 transcribes exactly for all eight parts (OPA189 1, OPA388 10, OPA333 1000, OPA187 500, OPA188 10, OPA186 500, OPA182 10, OPA387 10 kohm). p18 fig 6-1 gives OPA186 +/-5 pA typ at 25 C rising to +/-900 pA typ and +/-4.8 nA max at 125 C with the ESD-diode explanation, and the text states that the table 5-1 recommendation is correct for room temperature but lower impedances are required at 100 C. p19 eq 3 and eq 4 are as quoted, Example 1 works OPA186 at 100 C to 0.849 nA and R_MAX = 10 uV / 0.849 nA = 11.7 kohm, and the page says to keep source and feedback resistance below the table 5-1 value rather than rely on bias current cancellation because the transient amplitudes are not well balanced. p26 OPA333 row reads 10 uV, 0.05 uV/C, 0.35 MHz, 55 nV/rtHz, 1000 kohm, 20.4 kohm. opa333 p7 and p9 confirm the DC leg: IB +/-70 typ / +/-200 max pA at 25 C and +/-150 pA typ over temperature, and figs 7 and 8 keep the magnitude inside a roughly 50-150 pA band from -50 to 125 C, so the 240 kohm source in this block is limited by the transient ceiling and not by DC bias current. Envelope 1 kohm to 1 Mohm and its note are unchanged and still honest.

precision-buffer-rail-to-rail-output-flo.note: Re-read opa333 p7, p9, p13, p14 visually, pushing specifically on the load condition. The record does not commit the overreach it could have. The p7 table header reads At TA = 25 C, RL = 10 kohm connected to VS/2, VCM = VS/2 and VOUT = VS/2 unless otherwise noted, and the output block gives voltage output swing from rail 30 mV typ / 50 mV max at RL = 10 kohm plus 70 mV max at RL = 10 kohm over -40 to 125 C. The record carries RL = 10 kohm in the rule field, in the prose and in the citation note, and its claim that the whole DC page is measured into that same load is supported both by the header and by the AOL row repeating RL = 10 kohm. The light-load regime is handled rather than ignored: rule.light_load_helps is explicit, and p9 fig 6 output voltage swing vs output current does show the widest swing as IOUT approaches zero with each curve bending over as the output sources or sinks a few milliamps. Critically, the claim that the floor survives at near-zero load current is not a graph extrapolation - opa333 p13 section 7.3.4 states it load-independently: a good single-supply operational amplifier may swing close to single-supply ground but does not reach ground. The remedy is verbatim on p13 fig 19 (RP = 20 kohm from VOUT to a -5 V additional negative supply, more negative than the amplifier V-) and p14 (recommended resistor approximately 20 kohm; NOTE that it increases current consumption by several hundreds of microamps; accuracy excellent down to 0 V and as low as -2 mV with limiting and nonlinearity below -2 mV; resistances as low as 10 kohm give excellent accuracy to -10 mV). The 17 uA quiescent figure the cost is measured against is on p7. Envelope vout_min_v 0 to 0.1 V is anchored on the 50 mV and 70 mV spec values, and the envelope_note is explicit that the specific millivolts belong to one micropower CMOS RRO family while the mechanism - saturation voltage growing with output current, p9 fig 6 - is general.

precision-buffer-sar-charge-bucket-inter.note: Re-read sprpeo2 p22, p23, p26, p27, p28, p29 visually. All six citations are exact. p22 buffered vs unbuffered table transcribes verbatim: direct capacitor array connection, time-varying (switching) input impedance, significant charge injection, driver must handle transient currents, settling time critical. p23 unbuffered challenge panel lists impact on driver as requires low output impedance, must handle charge injection, needs adequate bandwidth for fast settling, complex input filter design (charge-bucket plus anti-aliasing). p26 states the two purposes side by side with the limitations box - charge bucket filter might not effectively stop aliasing, pure anti-aliasing filter might not be fast enough to settle the input, and for buffered ADCs charge bucket not needed - which is exactly the records conflict and not_needed_when fields. p27 carries all four formulas as written: C_FLT >= 20*C_SH >= 20*18 pF >= 360 pF taken to 470 pF, practical t_FLT_settle = t_ACQ = 12*tau_FLT, R_FLT = t_ACQ/(12*C_FLT) about 12 ohm, minimum driver GBW > 4*(1/(2*pi*R_FLT*C_FLT)), and confirming the RC combination plus driver in simulation is recommended. p28 EVM schematics match, and 10 ohm plus 1 nF for the unbuffered part is TI own summary line on p27; the record omits the 470 pF differential cap present in both dashed boxes but does not misstate anything. p29 comparison table gives series R 10-22 ohm, shunt C 470 pF-1 nF, source Z under 10 ohm, filter cutoff 15-33 MHz, min driver BW 25-30 MHz, all for the 16-bit 5 MSPS pair named on p24. Envelope load_kind switched-cap is sourced, not inferred - p26 is where the rule stops at a buffered-input ADC - and the envelope_note is honest that the absolute values belong to a 5 MSPS / 70 ns converter and do not transfer while the ratios and the step ordering do. Flagged for the designer rather than refuted: neither this record nor precision-buffer-capacitive-load-isolation says the SAME series resistor has to satisfy both the settling ceiling and the stability optimum, and for this block the two bounds cross - t_acq/(12*C) with t_acq = 9 us gives R <= 750 ohm at 1 nF and <= 1.6 kohm at 470 pF, while sboa418 eq 2 with R_O = 2 kohm and f_gbw = 350 kHz asks for about 1.2 kohm and 2.0 kohm respectively. Neither record over-claims exclusivity (one is a max, one is an optimum) and the checklist requires both classes, so the framing is not wrong, only silent on the collision.

precision-buffer-capacitive-load-isolati.note: Re-measured BOTH figures from scratch out of the PDF vector geometry and then cross-checked them against an independent 864-dpi raster pixel scan of the same pages, because this record has been edited twice and got worse in between. The current numbers are the right ones. opa333 p11 fig 15: the plot frame is the single path (97.73, 90.86) to (279.99, 214.32); 19 printed gridlines fit px = 6.684 + 91.033*log10(C_pF) with a max residual of 0.0034 decade, and the 7 interior horizontal gridlines sit on an exact 8-way split of the frame to within 0.023 pt, so frame bottom is 0 percent and frame top is 40 percent. The trace is exactly two cubic beziers, (99.42,214.17) to (204.17,171.68) to (260.07,91.28). Evaluated off that: span 10.44 pF to 607 pF, terminating at 39.9 percent on the frame top; 100 pF gives 9.74 percent, 300 pF gives 24.48 percent, 470 pF gives 33.68 percent, and 7 percent falls at 69.3 pF with 15 percent at 161.6 pF. The independent raster scan (curve runs isolated by stroke thickness, vertical gridline columns discarded) agrees to within 0.1 percentage point at every point tested - 69 pF 6.99, 100 pF 9.76 by interpolation across the decade gridline, 150 pF 14.04, 162 pF 15.06, 300 pF 24.5 by interpolation, 470 pF 33.70, 605 pF 39.63 - and finds zero curve pixels anywhere beyond 609 pF, so the trace really does stop there rather than being clipped or overpainted. On the overpaint trap specifically: exactly two paths overlap the fig 15 frame, the frame rect and the curve, and neither is a white fill, so there is no white rectangle inflating this read. The record is therefore right on all three counts that changed - 100 pF is about 10 percent not 7, 300 pF is about 25 percent not 15, and there is no 1000 pF point at all. sboa418 p9 fig 5-1: four 114-segment polylines, matched to phase margin by legend swatch colour (black 75, red 60, dark teal 45, cyan 30 - each swatch line sits on the vertical centre of its own legend text). y frame 343.47 = 0 V, 156.32 = 0.016 V on 8 equal divisions. All four traces start at 0.099 mV and end at 10.0875 mV, so the settled level is 10.09 mV as claimed. Peaks: 75 deg 10.0875 (no overshoot, its peak IS the settled level), 60 deg 11.0394, 45 deg 12.5261, 30 deg 14.3305 mV - the record's 10.09 / 11.04 / 12.53 / 14.33 exactly. On the nominal 10 mV step those are 10.4, 25.3 and 43.3 percent, which is the record's about 10, 25 and 43; against the 10.09 settled level they would be 9.4, 24.2 and 42.0, so the percentages are honest either way. The 30 deg trace does ring visibly - successive maxima 14.33, 10.87, 10.23, 10.11 mV. A white fill rect does exist on this page but it is the legend box at x greater than 348 and y greater than 288, nowhere near any peak. Every other citation re-read and exact: p2 fig 1-1 flat 120 ohm plus the electrical row R_O f = 1 MHz 120 ohm and the sentence limiting the analysis to amplifiers with a flat resistive output impedance; p4 fig 3-1 OPA392 buffer with C3 10u direct on the output, the Vout trace ringing across the full 0 to 1.00 ms axis, phase margin of less than 1 degree, and the ADC reference driver sentence; p5 eq 2 transcribed exactly, 380 mohm giving 60 degrees, and Always use Spice simulation tools such as TINA-TI to verify; p6 eq 3 with the 40 dB/decade rate of closure; p7 eq 4 and eq 5 with the 20 dB ROC restored; p8 fig 4-5 reading 4.99 V at 20 ohm and 4.90 V at 200 ohm into 10 kohm plus 5 nF from 5 V, plus the text that RISO is designed to be as small as tolerable and that a larger one costs voltage error and settling time; opa333 p7 Open-loop output impedance f = 350 kHz IO = 0 A 2 kohm and Gain-bandwidth product CL = 100 pF 350 kHz. p9 also supports the prose's optimally damped label - In certain cases, it is typical for a phase margin of 60 degrees to be considered optimally damped. The one inference in the record, that overshoot past 605 pF is worse than 40 percent, is a one-step monotone extrapolation off a trace that leaves the frame top still rising, and the record labels it unquantified rather than pretending to a number. Nothing here refutes.

precision-buffer-chopper-artifacts-into-.note: Re-read sprpeo2 p5 AND p6 side by side, plus sboa586a p11 and p25 and opa333 p13, pushing on the relocated clause. The p5 note is now right about both pages. p5 and p6 carry the SAME slide title, SAR ADC Acquisition and Conversion Phase, and the SAME schematic, and it is the in-figure red annotation that distinguishes them - p5 is annotated Acquisition Phase with S1 drawn CLOSED (its blade lying flat between the two contacts), p6 is annotated Conversion Phase with S1 drawn OPEN (blade lifted off the right contact). So the record's parenthetical - S1 opening, after which the comparator works on the single held C_SH voltage, is drawn on the next slide, p6 Conversion Phase - is exactly what the two pages show, and the imprecision flagged last pass is repaired. The basis it keeps on p5 is genuinely on p5: the balance cartoon has a SAMPLE AND HOLD block on one arm and a DAC block on the other, both resting on a block labelled COMPARATOR, and the schematic gives S1, R_SH, C_SH, S2, Comp, N-Bit CDAC and N-Bit Register with V_CSH(t) = V_CSH(t0) + [VIN - V_CSH(t0)]*(1 - exp(-t/tau)), tau = R_SH*C_SH, and the settling curve landing inside 1/2 LSB at t_AQ - so one C_SH voltage per conversion is sourced, not asserted. THE REST RE-CHECKED FROM SCRATCH. sboa586a p11 is verbatim: the bias current is typically 160pA, the measured transients are 2uA which is 12,500 times the magnitude of the bias current, the two large transients correspond to transitioning of the calibration circuit input switches, the smaller transient between the large transients occurs when the synchronous notch filter is switched, the period of the calibration cycle for this example is 1.54us (fchop = 650kHz), and Since these transients are currents, the impact of the transients can be minimized by reducing the source and feedback impedance. Fig 3-6 on the same page is annotated No 1/f Noise on a flat 9 nV/rtHz floor from 10 Hz out to about 20 kHz, then discrete tones under a bracket labelled Noise tones from chopping calibration with fchop 650kHz and 2fchop 1.3MHz called out and further harmonics to 10 MHz. sboa586a p25 fig 8-6 is OPA188 at G = 101 with the unfiltered blue trace spiking to about -12 and +8 uV RTI, the orange 1kohm + 22pF trace labelled 7.2 MHz clearly reduced, and the red 1kohm + 47pF trace labelled 3.4 MHz reduced further - the record pairs each RC with the right corner frequency and in the right improving order. Step 6 on that page is verbatim, including Chopping noise is of the greatest concern when the amplifier is in unity gain, with no external filter and Also, large source or feedback impedances increase the amplitude of the chopping noise. opa333 p13 section 7.3.3 is verbatim: an auto-calibration technique with a time-continuous 350-kHz operational amplifier in the signal path, zero-corrected every 8 us, approximately 100 us after power up to achieve specified VOS accuracy, This design has no aliasing or flicker noise. The record's reconciliation of that sentence with the white paper stands - the datasheet is claiming no noise folding inside the amplifier, not the absence of switching artifacts at the terminals, which is a different measurement on a different part. ONE IMPRECISION CARRIED OVER, still not load-bearing and still disclosed: the prose calls the fig 3-6 floor otherwise flat while the figure shows a broad hump peaking near 33 nV/rtHz around 150 kHz before the tones start. The source note describes that rise correctly (no 1/f region, a rise near 100 kHz, and discrete tones), the flicker-free half is the page's own annotation, and the record's rule is about periodic artifacts landing in a sampled code rather than about the shape of the floor. Envelope load_kind switched-cap is the right bound and the envelope_note argues it correctly. Verified.

precision-buffer-pin-decoupling-and-inpu.note: Re-read opa333 p23 and p9 visually. Every one of the four layout moves is on p23 in the vendors own words. Section 10.1.1 text: keep traces short and where possible use a printed-circuit-board ground plane with surface-mount components placed as close to the device pins as possible; place a 0.1-uF capacitor closely across the supply pins; and RFI can generally be identified as a variation in offset voltage or DC signal levels with changes in the interfering RF signal - which is the records symptom field almost verbatim. Figure 34 carries all four annotations the record cites: Use low-ESR ceramic bypass capacitor drawn twice, once at the VS+ / V+ node and once at the VS- side, both returned to the plane; Ground (GND) plane on another layer; Place components close to device and to each other to reduce parasitic errors on the RF/RG pair at the inverting pin; and Run the input traces as far away from the supply lines as possible, with the dashed box around the GND/VIN/RG/RF input network. p9 fig 4 shows CMRR near 127 dB at 1 Hz falling to about 20 dB by 100 kHz and fig 5 shows +PSRR near 118 dB and -PSRR near 105 dB at 1 Hz, both collapsing to about 20 dB by 100 kHz, so the quantitative reason for pin-local bypass holds. Envelope board_layers min 2 is a trivially sound inference from a plane on another layer, and the envelope_note says outright that it is about a reference plane and pin-adjacent space being available. Confirmed absent as claimed: no thermal EMF or Seebeck term, no guard ring, and no CMRR or PSRR referred-to-input arithmetic for a moving common mode anywhere in this record or in any other precision-buffer record - a grep of all bb-adc records, checklists and tasks finds those terms only in the resistive-attenuator and series-voltage-reference records for other blocks. Two minor notes, not refutations: near 110-120 dB at DC is a touch high for the -PSRR trace, which reads about 105 dB at 1 Hz, while the load-bearing half - both collapse to about 20 dB by 100 kHz - is right; and the record omits the same paragraphs claim that the OPA333 is specifically designed to minimize RFI susceptibility, which makes it read slightly more alarmist than the page, though the pages next sentence (strong RF fields may still cause varying offset levels) keeps the guidance valid.

precision-buffer-riso-settling-stability.note: Re-read sboa418 p2, p5, p9 and p11, sprpeo2 p26 and p27, and opa333 p7 and p11, re-derived every number from the raw formulas rather than accepting them, and re-measured fig 15 out of the vector geometry with an independent raster cross-check. Both things that were refuted last pass are fixed and nothing new breaks. ALGEBRA, all re-derived independently: ceilings t_ACQ/(12*C) with t_ACQ = 9 us give 750.00 ohm at 1 nF and 1595.74 ohm at 470 pF; eq 2 with R_O = 2 kohm and f_gbw = 350 kHz gives 1207.75 ohm and 1956.52 ohm; ratios 62.1 and 81.6 percent, the record's 62 and 82; the crossover where t/(12C) meets eq 2 reduces to sqrt(1 + 8*pi*R_O*C*f) = pi*f*t/3 - 1 and solves to 243.50 pF; the same equality solved for f at C = 1 nF gives 778.09 kHz, the record's 778.1 kHz and about 0.8 MHz; and 20*48 pF = 960 pF, so the crossover really does sit under the C floor. The 48 pF is a block input rather than a claim about a cited page, and it is factual - the ADS8326 datasheet in this workspace states the 48 pF sampling capacitance on p7 and p21. THE TWO NEW CITATIONS CARRY THE WORDS CLAIMED. sboa418 p9 reads verbatim: the optimal isolation resistance is the smallest series resistance that produces an acceptable transient response when driving the capacitive load; While a phase margin of 45 degrees is generally considered stable, this may not be sufficient for applications that demand low overshoot; In certain cases, it is typical for a phase margin of 60 degrees to be considered optimally damped; If voltage error is of primary concern, a phase margin of 45 degrees can be targeted as this allows the smallest isolation resistance to be used; and Selecting an RISO resistance that places fz1 exactly at the closure frequency, targets a phase margin between 50-60 degrees. The same page also carries the buffer caveat the envelope_note leans on - For a typical amplifier in a buffer configuration, the closure frequency is simply the gain bandwidth of the op amp - together with the qualifier that for a loaded AOL the closure frequency is always less than the gain bandwidth, which the record's own p9 note states. sboa418 p11 reads verbatim: Equation 13 can be used to quickly derive the isolation resistance required to target 50-60 degrees of phase margin. Spice simulation tools such as TINA-TI must be used to verify the resultant phase margin, as this can vary considerable depending on the initial phase margin and other circuit conditions - the sic on considerable is the document's own typo. Eq 13 on that page is eq 2 restated and eq 14 is the gain-stage variant; a scan of all 14 pages for 45 finds it only in p3 prose (45 degrees is a common benchmark, designers commonly target a minimum of 45) and in p9 prose and the fig 5-1 legend, so the record's claim that the document publishes NO closed form for the 45-degree R is exact. THE REWRITTEN TEST NOW STOPS WHERE THE SOURCES STOP. rule.test is a screen that fires a phase-margin check at the ceiling R; eq2_is_not_a_maximum is p9 in p9's own words; reject_when defers BOTH of its conditions - the 45-degree R and the ringing inside the accuracy window - to simulation, which is precisely what sboa418 p11 (Spice must be used) and sprpeo2 p27 (confirming RC combination plus driver in simulation recommended) demand. No part is rejected on unsimulated algebra any more, and the 470 pF case that made the old wording unsupportable at 82 percent of the optimum is now handled by the same screen rather than a verdict.
